content: Cigarette smoking significantly increases the risk of severe adverse effects associated with the use of the contraceptive patch, such as heart attacks, blood clots, and strokes. This risk is particularly elevated in women over the age of 35 and in those who smoke heavily (15 or more cigarettes per day). If you are using the contraceptive patch, you should not smoke. The norelgestromin and ethinyl estradiol transdermal system, commonly referred to as the contraceptive patch, is prescribed to prevent pregnancy. It contains two hormones: norelgestromin, a progestin, and ethinyl estradiol, an estrogen. These hormones work together to inhibit ovulation (the release of eggs from the ovaries), alter the cervical mucus to make it more difficult for sperm to reach the egg, and modify the uterine lining to prevent implantation. While the contraceptive patch is highly effective in preventing pregnancy, it does not protect against HIV or other sexually transmitted infections. The contraceptive patch is applied to the skin and is used in a 4-week cycle. A new patch is applied once a week for three consecutive weeks, followed by a patch-free week during which menstruation typically occurs. It is essential to follow the instructions provided by your healthcare provider or pharmacist precisely. If you are starting the patch for the first time, you may apply it on the first day of your menstrual period or the first Sunday after your period begins. If you start the patch after the first day of your period, you must use an additional method of contraception, such as condoms or spermicide, for the first seven days of the initial cycle. Always apply the patch on the same day of the week, referred to as the Patch Change Day. During the fourth week, remove the patch and do not apply a new one. Begin a new 4-week cycle by applying a new patch the day after the patch-free week ends, even if your period has not started or has not finished. Do not go more than seven days without wearing a patch. The patch should be applied to clean, dry, intact skin on the buttock, abdomen, upper outer arm, or upper torso, avoiding areas that may be irritated, cut, or exposed to tight clothing. Do not place the patch on the breasts. Avoid applying creams, lotions, powders, or other topical products to the area where the patch is applied. Rotate the application site with each new patch to minimize skin irritation. Do not cut, alter, or decorate the patch, and do not use additional adhesives to secure it. To apply the patch, open the foil pouch carefully, peel off the clear plastic liner, and avoid touching the adhesive side. Press the patch firmly onto the skin for 10 seconds, ensuring the edges adhere well. After one week, remove the patch, fold it in half with the adhesive sides together, and dispose of it in a trash can out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush the patch down the toilet. If the patch becomes partially or completely detached for less than one day, reapply it immediately or replace it with a new patch if it is no longer sticky. If skin irritation occurs at the application site, you may remove the patch and apply a new one to a different area. Before using the contraceptive patch, inform your doctor if you are allergic to estrogens, progestins, or any other medications. Notify your healthcare provider if you are using other hormonal contraceptives, such as pills, rings, injections, or implants, as they will advise you on transitioning to the patch. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, supplements, and herbal products you are taking, as some may interact with the patch. Medications such as antibiotics, antifungals, seizure medications, and herbal products like St. John’s wort may reduce the effectiveness of the patch. The patch may not be suitable for individuals with these conditions. Additionally, inform your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you suspect pregnancy while using the patch, contact your doctor immediately. The contraceptive patch delivers a higher average level of estrogen into the bloodstream compared to oral contraceptives, which may increase the risk of blood clots. Studies have shown conflicting results regarding this risk. Discuss with your doctor whether the patch is the most appropriate contraceptive method for you. If you forget to apply or change your patch, follow specific instructions based on the timing of the missed dose. Missing a patch at the start of a cycle or for more than two days during the cycle may reduce its effectiveness, and backup contraception should be used for one week. Mild side effects of the patch may include skin irritation at the application site, breast tenderness, nausea, weight changes, acne, or changes in menstrual flow. Severe side effects, such as sudden headaches, vision changes, chest pain, or signs of blood clots, require immediate medical attention. The patch may also increase the risk of certain cancers, gallbladder disease, and liver tumors. Discuss these risks with your doctor. Store the patch at room temperature, away from heat and moisture, and out of reach of children. Dispose of expired or unused patches properly. In case of overdose, remove all patches and contact poison control or emergency services. Inform laboratory personnel that you are using the patch, as it may interfere with certain tests. Do not share your medication with others, and consult your pharmacist or doctor with any questions.
